column5: description
Average age of parents of the current cohort (i.e., of cohort of newborn individuals in the population). Generation length reflects the turnover rate of breeding individuals in a population.
Average length of life or life expectancy of a population
Categorical description (days, months, etc.) of life or life expectancy of a population
The life stage that makes up the greatest proportion of an individual's life span
Time to maturity, including the time spent as dormant larval forms, aestivation and holometabolous taxa
Categorical description (days, months, etc.) of time to maturity, including the time spent as dormant larval forms, aestivation and holometabolous taxa
Area within a species' EOO, excluding cases of vagrancy (IUCN 2001). See https://www.ala.org.au/spatial-portal-help/aoo/.

Area contained within the shortest continuous imaginary boundary that encompasses all known, inferred, or projected sites of present occurrence of a taxon, excluding cases of vagrancy (IUCN 2012). For migratory species, EOO should be based on the minimum of breeding or non-breeding (wintering) areas, but not both. See https://www.ala.org.au/spatial-portal-help/aoo/.
The area in which an individual of a species lives and moves on a periodic basis
Description of the extent of the area occupied by all individuals of a species (including migratory range)

Description of subpopulation connectivity (combination of distribution and connectivity) for a species within a landscape. Connectivity can be infuenced by taxon specific features, such as habitat specialisation or dispersal ability, of from landscape features, such as vegetation clearance.
Nature of dependency (generalist/specialist) of a taxon on other organisms for a part of its life or to complete some aspect of its lifecycle
Role played by a taxon in the formation and maintenance of its ecosystem

Reliance of a taxon on specific and/or narrow biotic or abiotic habitat features for breeding, foraging, nesting, or living. It also includes reliance on a habitat through which a species may be moving.
Ability of the organism to occupy a new site
Strategy used for obtaining food source
Reliance of an individual, or part of an individual's life stage, on some aspect of fire, such as fire ephemerals, burnt wood, etc.
The ability of an organism to detect fire or an aspect of fire
Evidence of emigration and/or immigration in response to fire event(s)
Physiological maximum potential reproductive output of an individual (usually female) over its known lifetime, measured by number of eggs, or young
Degree (high/low) of the physiological maximum potential reproductive output of an individual (usually female) over its known lifetime

Reproductive output of an individual (usually female) during a single reproductive event within the known lifetime of the individual/species/taxon, usually measured as the number of eggs, or young. This is also used if lifetime of the individual/species/taxon is unknown, for example, in 'long-lived' taxa

Degree (high/low) of the reproductive output of an individual (usually female) during a single reproductive event within the known lifetime of the individual/species/taxon. This is also used if lifetime of the individual/species/taxon is unknown, for example, in 'long-lived' taxa
The degree of development of the offspring at birth/hatching and the subsequent parental investment required to raise offspring
Frequency of reproductive events
Flexibility for opportunistic reproductive output
Mode of reproduction

The timing of seasonal or cyclic variation in life cycle events, across a species' life that are influenced by seasonal and interannual variations in climate, i.e., timing of developmental cycles, hibernation, etc.
Microhabitat(s) with which a species actively interacts, including movement specifically around, or associated with that microhabitat, such as for foraging, lekking, etc.
Microhabitat(s) in which a species nests, incuding habitats where a life stage matures
Microhabitat(s) in which a species shelters
Shape of the body, e.g., dorsoventrally flattened
Longest width or diameter of the shell perpendicular to the shell axis in land snails
Longest distance between the apex and the base of the aperture parallel to the shell axis in land snails
Length of the body as taken from most anterior point to most posterior point of main body segments, not including wings or legs
Length of the body and wings as taken from most anterior point of the main body segments to the most posterior point of protruding wings
Length between the rear of the eye socket to the centre rear of the carapace in crayfish
Length of forewing
Length of hindwing
Presence of protective integument (e.g., exoskeleton or shell) that may provide protection against dessication
Distance across the thorax between the base of the wings
Length of leg
Mass of an individual
Degree of development of wings
Length of wing when not specified as hindwing or forewing

The extent of reliance of a species on a specific microhabitat through which it can dipserse, e.g., inability to cross open ground, alien mosaic habitats, contrasted to a species that can cross a range of habitats
Categorical descriptions (high/low) of how far an individual can move, per dispersal event, from the location of an existing population
Speed of movement of an individual through the landscape
Mode of movement through the landscape

The length of time in which individuals or progules of a species, or a life stage, is dispersive. For example, a species may only be dispersive for a restricted and discrete period (i.e., as a juvenile); it may be dispersive throughout its life, but restricted to specific times i.e., seasonally; or it may be flexibly dispersive throughout its life.
Distance travelled to reach migration site
Categorical descriptions (long/short) of distance travelled to reach migration site
Frequency of migration in a species' lifetime
A species' fidelity for each migratory destination; for example, species with high migration_site_fidelity would return to the exact same location at each migration event.
Physiological tolerance to abiotic factors such as temperature, humidity, hydrology
Lethal temperature 50; the temperature at which 50% of the sample dies
Lethal temperature 100; the temperature at which 100% of the sample dies
Critical thermal maximum; the upper thermal limit of organisms, the point at which organised movement and function stops and the organism dies
Critical thermal 50; the temperature at which 50% of organisms meet their thermal limit, at which organised movement and function stops and the organism dies
Critical thermal minimum; the minimum thermal limit of organisms, the point at which organised movement and function stops and the organism dies
